newsitem.title: USA: Signs of hope bloom in flood-ravaged Grand Forks.
newsitem.headline: Signs of hope bloom in flood-ravaged Grand Forks.

text.p: Officials gave permission on Sunday for residents to return to their homes temporarily in nearly three-quarters of flood-ravaged Grand Forks and said a key bridge may soon be re-opened.

Signs of progress, however, did not diminish the enormous clean-up task ahead. There still was no power or drinking water in Grand Forks or neighbouring East Grand Forks, Minnesota, and visits to flooded homes were restricted to daylight hours.

Grand Forks officials said the Red River of the North had receeded far enough so that 70 percent of the city was now open to those who wanted to check out their property and begin cleaning up -- but not to return permanently. The Red Cross was assembling 30,000 clean-up kits to assist.

In East Grand Forks, where all 9,000 residents have been out of their homes for more than a week, city officials said many homes would have to be rebuilt. They said they hoped to set up a trailer park or another form of temporary housing to accommodate displaced people.

Sunday was also the first time some East Grand Forks residents were allowed back in the city for brief inspection tours. A small section in the northeast part of town was opened for a three-hour period.

Grand Forks engineers inspected the Kennedy Bridge, one of three spans crossing the Red between North Dakota and Minnesota, and said no structural damage had occurred. They said the bridge may be re-opened to traffic Monday though the other two bridges linking the towns remain closed.

A Northwest Airlines Boeing 747 landed at Grand Forks Air Force Base Sunday carrying 200,000 pounds of supplies and other donations raised by 21 radio stations in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area. The Salvlation Army planned to distribute the relief items.

The Red, swollen by runoff from one of the heaviest snowfalls on record, overwhelmed levees in the Grand Forks area about 10 days ago, forcing more than 50,000 people from their homes. Fire later ravaged several blocks of downtown Grand Forks.

Officials said 20,000 people in the Grand Forks area had applied for federal assistance so far. No deaths have been attributed directly to the flooding in the Grand Forks area and police said burglaries and looting have not been a problem even though thousands of structures have been left vacant.

Upstream at Fargo and nearby Moorhead, Minnesota, officials said damage could be as much as $7 million, even though that area escaped the massive destuction that hit Grand Forks -- where unofficial estimates have placed damage as high as $1 billion.

Fargo officials said their battle required 3.5 million sandbags -- more than 10 times what they had expected to use. The bags will be collected during the next few weeks and the sand recycled for use as building material or stored to be put on icy and snow-packed roads next winter.
In Canada, over 17,000 people have been evacuated from southern Manitoba, with many taking refuge in a Winnipeg sports arena, because of the rising Red River.
In Winnipeg, a city of 650,000 people, a massive effort was underway to shore itself up for the torrent slowly headed its way.
